newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Australia said facing new iron ore boom.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Australia said facing new iron ore boom.

text.p: Australian iron ore production is expected to rise at least 20 percent to about 170 million tonnes a year by 2005 with over three-quarters for shipment to Asia, North Ltd managing director Campbell Anderson said.

To meet demand Australian iron ore miners would need to expand existing operations, develop new mines and implement major infrastructure refurbishment, he told an Australia-Japan Business Co-operation Committees meeting on Tuesday.
The forecast was based mainly on the emergence of rapidly growing steel industries in South Korea, Taiwan and China.
These posed a challenge to Japan's steelmakers in export markets, Anderson said.
"Australia's iron ore miners too must respond to the needs of the changing marketplace," Anderson told the meeting, the main formal event in the Australia-Japan trade calendar.

In the same session, Rokuro Suehiro, representative director and executive vice-president of Japan's biggest steelmaker Nippon Steel Corp, indirectly floated the prospect of a role by Japan in the development of new resource projects in Australia for the non-Japanese Asian export market.

"We believe that Japan, as a stable buyer of steelmaking raw materials and energy and a potential provider of capital, will be able to cooperate in resource development in Australia," Suehiro said. But the Nippon Steel executive presented a prospect of flat steel production in Japan.

Estimated total crude steel production in the second half of the present fiscal year, which ends March 31, 1997, would be about 49 million tonnes, steady with the slightly more than 49 million tonnes output in the first half, he said.
This would be down from last year's annual production of 100.02 million tonnes, a decrease of about two percent, he said.
It was estimated the Japanese steel production would remain at 97-98 million tonnes a year, Suehiro said.
Despite a moderate economic upturn in Japan, steel product stocks had accumulated because of increased production in anticipation of demand from the Hanshin earthquake last year.

While Japanese automobiles produced overseas had doubled to nearly six million units from the late 1980s, the export of automobiles from Japan had decreased dramatically to 3.5 million units from 6.0 million units, Suehiro said.
Domestic production was down to slightly more than 10 million units at present from 13.59 million in fiscal 1990.
Production of electrical appliances also had shifted oversaeas, Suehiro said.

But he said that towards the years 2000 or 2005, new steelworks planned for Korea, Taiwan and Southeast Asia led to a predicted "extreme increase" in demand for steelmaking raw materials, as well as for energy.
"We believe that the importance of Australia as a source of resource supply will be enhanced more and more," he said.
At the same time, Suehiro criticised industrial disputes in Australia's coal industry but praised relative stability in the iron ore industry.

Japanese customers had cancelled coal contracts or made urgent procurements from other sources, while the ratio of iron ore purchased by Japan from Australia had increased by about five percent in the past 10 years, Suehiro said.

Last year, 45 million tonnes, or one-third, of Australian iron ore products were shipped to China, South Korea and Taiwan, up from 15 million tonners or 15 percent a decade ago, North's Anderson said.
The commitment of Japanese customers had been crucial in the past and that support will be required in the future, he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
